title: History of China
wiki_lead:
The history of China spans several millennia across a wide geographical area. Chinese civilization originated in the Yellow and Yangtze river basins, evolving into one of the world's oldest cradles of civilization. Traditional historiography views this past through the lens of the dynastic cycle. The earliest confirmed historical period begins with the Shang dynasty (c. 1250 BC), which left the oldest surviving oracle bone inscriptions. It was followed by the Zhou dynasty (c. 1046 – 256 BC), an era that introduced the Mandate of Heaven and laid the philosophical foundations for Confucianism, Taoism, and Legalism.
China was first unified under a centralized imperial state by Qin Shi Huang in 221 BC. The subsequent Han dynasty (202 BC – 220 AD) established a long-lasting imperial order, institutionalized Confucianism, and fostered major technological advancements such as paper-making. Following centuries of disunity that saw the spread of Buddhism, imperial unity was restored by the Sui dynasty (581–618) and the Tang dynasty (618–907), a golden age of poetry, culture, and cosmopolitan trade. The Song dynasty (960–1279) followed, driving major advancements in woodblock printing, technology, and the imperial examination system.
In the 13th century, the Mongol Empire conquered China and established the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368). Han rule returned with the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), noted for maritime exploration, arts, and major restoration of the Great Wall and Grand Canal. The final imperial lineage, the Manchu-led Qing dynasty (1644–1912), expanded China's territory to its imperial peak before suffering severe internal instability and military defeats to foreign powers in the 19th century.
The 1911 Revolution ended imperial rule and established the Republic of China (ROC). Decades of conflict followed, including the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Chinese Civil War. In 1949, Mao Zedong, leader of the Chinese Communist Party, proclaimed the People's Republic of China (PRC) on the mainland, while the ROC government retreated to Taiwan. Following the Cultural Revolution, the PRC instituted reform and opening up under Deng Xiaoping starting in 1978, transforming the country into the world's fastest-growing major economy.

Prehistory


Paleolithic (1.7 Ma – 12 ka)

The archaic human species of Homo erectus arrived in Eurasia sometime between 1.3 and 1.8 million years ago (Ma) and numerous remains of its subspecies have been found in what is now China. The oldest of these is the southwestern Yuanmou Man (元谋人; in Yunnan), dated to c. 1.7 Ma, which lived in a mixed bushland-forest environment alongside chalicotheres, deer, the elephant Stegodon, rhinos, cattle, pigs, and the giant short-faced hyena. The better-known Peking Man (北京猿人; near Beijing) of 700,000–400,000 BP, was discovered in the Zhoukoudian cave alongside scrapers, choppers, and, dated slightly later, points, burins, and awls. Other Homo erectus fossils have been found widely throughout the region, including the northwestern Lantian Man in Shaanxi, as well minor specimens in northeastern Liaoning and southern Guangdong. The dates of most Paleolithic sites were long debated but have been more reliably established based on modern magnetostratigraphy: Majuangou at 1.66–1.55 Ma, Lanpo at 1.6 Ma, Xiaochangliang at 1.36 Ma, Xiantai at 1.36 Ma, Banshan at 1.32 Ma, Feiliang at 1.2 Ma and Donggutuo at 1.1 Ma. Evidence of fire use by Homo erectus occurred between 1–1.8 million years BP at the archaeological site of Xihoudu, Shanxi Province.
The circumstances surrounding the evolution of Homo erectus to contemporary H. sapiens is debated; the three main theories include the dominant "Out of Africa" theory (OOA), the regional continuity model and the admixture variant of the OOA hypothesis. grok_lead: The history of China comprises the recorded experiences of a civilization with one of the longest continuous cultural traditions, extending over 3,500 years from the advent of writing during the Shang dynasty (c. 1600â1046 BCE) to the present People's Republic of China. Archaeological evidence reveals complex Neolithic societies predating this, such as those at Jiahu and Hemudu, but dynastic historiography traditionally begins with the semi-legendary Xia (c. 2070â1600 BCE), transitioning to the Bronze Age Shang era confirmed by oracle bone inscriptions that document royal divinations, ancestor worship, and early state administration. Subsequent periods feature the Zhou dynasty's feudal fragmentation (c. 1046â256 BCE), marked by philosophical developments including Confucianism and Legalism, followed by the short-lived but pivotal Qin unification in 221 BCE under Qin Shi Huang, who standardized weights, measures, script, and laws while initiating massive infrastructure projects like the early Great Wall and imperial mausoleum guarded by the Terracotta Army. The Han dynasty (206 BCEâ220 CE) established enduring institutions such as the imperial examination system and expanded territory through the Silk Road, fostering economic and cultural exchanges that also facilitated the introduction of Buddhism from the Indian subcontinent into China; the Sui dynasty (581â618 CE) reunified the divided empire, followed by eras like Tang (618â907 CE) and Song (960â1279 CE) that saw peaks in poetry, painting, urbanization, and technological innovation, including the four great inventionsâpapermaking, woodblock printing, gunpowder, and the magnetic compassâthat disseminated globally via trade routes. Dynastic cycles of centralization, corruption, rebellion, and replacement, often rationalized by the Mandate of Heaven concept, characterized imperial rule, interrupted by foreign conquests like the Mongol Yuan (1271â1368), the native restoration under the Ming dynasty (1368â1644), and Manchu Qing (1644â1912), which nonetheless integrated into Sinic frameworks while extending borders to historic maxima. The 19th and 20th centuries brought existential challenges: Qing stagnation amid Western imperialism, including the Opium Wars and unequal treaties, sparked the 1911 Revolution ending millennia of monarchy and ushering in republican chaos, warlordism, and Japanese aggression during the 1930sâ1940s. Civil war between Nationalists and Communists concluded with the latter's victory in 1949, founding the People's Republic under Mao Zedong, whose policies like the Great Leap Forward (1958â1962) induced catastrophic famine killing tens of millions, followed by the Cultural Revolution (1966â1976) that purged intellectuals and disrupted society. Post-Mao reforms from 1978 emphasized market liberalization, propelling rapid industrialization and poverty reduction but also environmental degradation, demographic imbalances from the one-child policy, and authoritarian consolidation under the Chinese Communist Party.
